sentences.text: The holotype fossil consists only of the front part of a snout.
In side view, the snout is rounded, while the front is expanded and flat when viewed from the front.
The snout bears no crest, and the palate curves upwards.
The first pair of teeth is located at the very tip of the snout.
The second and third pairs of teeth point obliquely sideways, contributing to a unique combination of traits.
Camposipterus nasutus displays a unique dental density of three teeth per three centimeters at the front of the jaw and 2.5 teeth at the rear.
Seeley speculated that a depression on the snout might serve for lip attachment, but pterosaurs instead had horny coverings.

Harry Govier Seeley originally named the species Ptenodactylus nasutus in 1869 based on fossils from Haslingfield, Cambridgeshire, while Richard Owen named Pterodactylus sedgwickii in 1859 based on the front part of a snout from the Cambridge Greensand.

Taissa Rodrigues and Alexander Kellner established the genus Camposipterus in 2013 after determining the species was distinct from Anhanguera fittoni, and the genus name honors Brazilian paleontologist Diogenes de Almeida Campos and the Greek word for wing.
The holotype specimen was found in the Cambridge Greensand, which dates to the Cenomanian but likely contains older Albian fossils.

In 2013, Rodrigues and Kellner transferred two additional species into the genus, though the question mark in the species names indicates that the authors were not certain about the validity of transferring those species.
Camposipterus(?) sedgwickii was reassigned to the genus Aerodraco in 2020.
Rodrigues and Kellner assigned Camposipterus to the clade Anhangueria but placed it incertae sedis due to an unknown position, meaning its exact position is uncertain.
A 2019 study by Jacobs et al. placed Camposipterus within the family Ornithocheiridae as the sister taxon of Cimoliopterus.
Some cladistic analyses suggested Camposipterus was more derived than Cimoliopterus but less derived than Cearadactylus atrox.
Rodrigues and Kellner treated Camposipterus as a clade defined by a unique combination of traits rather than a single shared derived character.
Camposipterus was a pterodactyloid pterosaur found in England, belongs to the parent group Anhangueria, and is classified as a reptile.
There are three recorded fossil occurrences of Camposipterus in the Paleobiology Database.
Researchers express uncertainty regarding the validity of assigning certain species to the genus Camposipterus.
In 2025, Pêgas assigned O. colorhinus to the genus Cimoliopterus based on its close relationship to C. cuvieri.
